items.title: Delegation to agents is the clinical risk worth watching
items.body: Fukuyama's worry is less runaway superintelligence than people handing agents everything, from email to targeting, because delegation is how hierarchies work. In a surgery the equivalent is quiet: an AI scribe drafts the note, a triage tool ranks the inbox, a coding tool suggests the codes, and each step is signed off a little faster than the last. The safeguard is the same as it has always been, a named clinician who actually reads the output and owns it.

items.title: White-collar work goes first, and that includes ours
items.body: If Fukuyama is right that symbolic-manipulation work is devalued before manual work, then letters, coding, summaries and form-filling are exposed well before consultation itself. For general practice that argues for being deliberate: let the tools take the paperwork, and protect the time freed for the parts of the job that are hard to automate, the judgement and the relationship.

items.title: Public mood matters for consent
items.body: With only about a third of Americans expecting AI to mostly help, and UK patients unlikely to be far more enthusiastic, a practice using an AI scribe should expect to explain it plainly. Telling patients what it does, what it does not do, and that a doctor checks the record costs a minute and buys trust. There is no clean Zitron contrast here; this edition is about attitudes, not economics.
